_guide.what this file is: The schema for one exercise, with a worked example under it. Copy this file, replace the example with your topic, check it with scripts/validate-spec.mjs, then paste the object from "meta" down into the spec island of assets/exercise.html.
_guide.how it becomes a page: The object from "meta" down is the spec. It is pasted into the <script type="application/json" id="spec"> island inside assets/exercise.html. Keys starting with _ are ignored by the page. Run the validator on the file before you paste: node scripts/validate-spec.mjs <spec.json>.
_guide.the one rule above all: Pick the interaction that teaches this idea best. Ask yourself what the student should DO to learn it, then pick the kind. A quiz is right for some ideas and wrong for many others. A process wants order, a set of categories wants sort, a pair of ideas that look alike wants match, and anything that changes or relates numbers wants a widget.
_guide.rule: nothing reveals before submit: No prompt, option list, figure or widget may show an answer before the student submits. The page grades on submit and then shows feedback.
_guide.rule: write simply: Short sentences. Common words. Explain a term the first time it is used. This holds for the page copy and for every prompt, feedback and misconception string here. A reader whose first language is not English must follow it easily.
_guide.rule: no em dashes: Do not use the long dash (the em dash) anywhere in this file. Use a comma, a colon, or two sentences.
_guide.meta.title: What the student sees as the page heading. Plain and specific, no marketing.
_guide.meta.slug: Lowercase repo and folder name: letters, digits, single hyphens. It becomes the GitHub repo name and so the URL.
_guide.meta.goal: One sentence starting 'After this you can ...'. It names the one capability the exercise trains. See rule 8 in references/learning-science.md.
_guide.meta.minutes: Honest length of one sitting. 6 to 12 steps fits a 10 minute phone session (rule 12).
_guide.meta.criterion.text: The bar in the student's words. The intro and the results screen both show it (rule 10).
_guide.meta.criterion.minCorrect: How many graded steps must be right for the criterion to count as met. Graded steps only: an explore step is never counted. Keep this number in agreement with the text.
_guide.steps: 6 to 12 steps for a 10 minute exercise. Order them so neighbouring steps do not all ask the same shape of question, and so sub-topics alternate (rule 5).
_guide.steps[].id: Short stable id, unique in the file. The results screen uses it to name a missed step.
_guide.steps[].kind: One of choice, multi, short, order, sort, match, explore. See the table below.
_guide.steps[].prompt: The question or the doing instruction. It must never contain or hint at the answer (rule 1).
_guide.steps[].tag: Author-only label for the sub-topic, used to interleave instead of blocking one idea together (rule 5). The page never renders it. It does not appear anywhere the student can see.
_guide.steps[].feedback: Required on every graded kind. Explains WHY the answer is right, shown after every attempt, right or wrong. Explain the mechanism, not the verdict (rule 2).
_guide.steps[].misconception: Required on choice and multi. The tempting wrong belief and why it fails, shown only after a wrong attempt (rule 3). Write one string for the whole step, or an object keyed by wrong option index with an optional "default".
_guide.steps[].hint: Optional. One nudge behind a Hint button. Put hints on the early steps of an idea, then drop them so the last step on that idea is free recall (rule 6).
_guide.steps[].figure: Optional, and it may decorate any step. A visual shown above the prompt: { "type": "svg" | "html" | "code", "content": "<markup or code text>", "caption": "optional" }. For "svg" and "html" the content is injected as markup. For "code" the content is shown in a code block.
_guide.figure reveal: Any element inside a figure may carry data-reveal="some caption text". That element becomes tappable, and hoverable on a desktop, and toggles its caption. This is the tap-or-hover-to-learn-more move. Use it for a diagram whose parts each need a name.
_guide.steps[].widget: Optional on any step, required on explore. An interactive play area: { "html": "<markup>", "controls": [ ... ], "js": "function (values, root) { ... }", "caption": "optional" }.
_guide.widget.controls[]: Each control is one of: { "type": "range", "name", "label", "min", "max", "step", "value", "unit": optional }, { "type": "switch", "name", "label", "value": true|false }, { "type": "select", "name", "label", "options": [ ... ], "value" }.
_guide.widget.js: The page renders the controls, holds the current values keyed by control name, and calls this function once at load and again on every change. It receives (values, root), where root is the play area element. Update the DOM inside root from here. That is how a simulation is built.
_guide.kind choice: Tap one option. Needs options (3 to 5 strings, each believable) and answer (the zero based index of the right one). Submits on tap. Order the options so the right one is not always in the same place.
_guide.kind multi: Tap all that apply. Needs options (a string array) and answer (an array of the indices that are correct: all of them and only them). Submits on a button.
_guide.kind short: Type the answer from memory. Needs answer as one accepted string, or an array of accepted strings. Matching ignores case, collapses spaces, and ignores trailing punctuation. Submits on a button.
_guide.kind order: Tap the items in the right order, with undo. Needs options (a string array, already in the order shown to the student) and answer (the correct order, as indices into options: a permutation of 0 to length minus 1). Submits on a button. Use it when the idea is a sequence or a decision order.
_guide.kind sort: Put each item into a bucket. Needs buckets (2 or 3 names) and items (a list of { "text", "bucket" }, where bucket is the correct bucket index). Submits on a button. Use it when the idea is 'which family does this belong to'.
_guide.kind match: Pair each left item with a right item. Needs lefts, rights (both string arrays, rights in display order) and answer (answer[i] is the correct index into rights for lefts[i]). Submits on a button. Use it when two sets of things are easily confused with each other.
_guide.kind explore: Ungraded, and it needs a widget. The page shows the widget and a Continue button. Nothing is scored here and nothing is counted in minCorrect. Put an explore step early when the student should play with the system before you ask anything about it (rule 13).
_guide.which kind to reach for: choice: one right answer among plausible rivals. multi: several things at once are true. short: the student must produce the word or number with no options in front of them. order: the sequence or the decision order matters. sort: items fall into families. match: two lists are easy to mix up. explore: a system has parts, a trade-off, or a number that moves.

meta.title: HTTP status codes
meta.goal: After this you can decide what to do next when a request fails, by reading its status code.

criterion.text: Get at least 6 of the 8 graded steps right.

steps.prompt: Slide the code and watch the family under it. Play here first, then answer the questions.

widget.html:
404

4xx: the request is wrong

There is nothing at that address.
widget.caption: Every code sits in a family, and the family says whose problem it is.

steps.prompt: A request arrives with no login at all. Which code comes back?
steps.feedback: 401 means the request carried no usable credentials, so the server asks who are you. 403 means the server knows who you are and still refuses.

misconception.1: 403 sounds more severe, so it is tempting. But 403 means the server recognized you and denied you. No credentials at all is 401.
misconception.3: 500 means the server broke. Nothing broke here: the request simply arrived without a login.

steps.hint: One of these two codes is about identity, and the other is about permission.

steps.prompt: Which family of codes says the request itself was wrong? Write the family.
steps.feedback: 4xx is the request's fault: the server read it and refused it. The server blames itself with 5xx.
steps.misconception: Most people answer 5xx, because a failed request feels like a server problem. 5xx means the request was fine and the server could not finish the job.

figure.caption: The reply the server sends when it wants a login.

steps.hint: Count the families from 1xx up. The one that blames the sender is the fourth.

steps.prompt: A request failed. Tap the checks in the order a client should try them.
options: Send the request again after a short wait
Fix the bytes the server refused
Refresh the token and send again
steps.feedback: Read the family first, because it decides everything else. 401 needs a new token, 4xx needs a different request, 5xx is worth one careful retry with a growing wait.
steps.misconception: Retrying first is the common mistake. A retry on a 400 sends the same broken bytes again, and the server answers the same way.

steps.prompt: Pair each code with what the server is telling you.
rights: You are not allowed to do that
The bytes you sent do not parse
There is nothing at that address
steps.feedback: Two of these look identical until you ask one question: did the server know who you were? 401 says no, 403 says yes and still no.
steps.misconception: 401 and 403 get swapped constantly, because both read as refusals. Keep the test in mind: 401 is about who you are, 403 is about what you may do.

steps.prompt: Put each code in the bucket that says who has to fix the problem.
steps.feedback: The first digit is the whole story. 4xx blames the request, 5xx blames the server, and 2xx and 3xx mean the request was handled.
steps.misconception: 404 gets filed under the server, because the page is missing. But the request asked for an address that is not there, so the fix is on the request side.

figure.caption: Tap a block to read what its family decides.

steps.hint: Only the first digit matters for this question.

steps.prompt: You are logged in as a student. You ask for another student's invoice and your role may not open it. Which code fits?
steps.feedback: You are known, so it is not 401, and the server refuses the action, so it is 403. A 200 with an empty page would hide the refusal, and a redirect would not explain it.

misconception.1: 401 means no usable credentials. You have credentials. They just do not grant this resource.
misconception.2: A 200 with nothing in it tells the client nothing and hides a real decision.

steps.prompt: Which of these mean the client should change the request before sending it again?
steps.feedback: Both are 4xx, so the request needs a fix: different bytes, or a different address. The others either worked or are the server's own problem.

misconception.2: 500 and 502 look like failures, so they feel like something to fix. They are the server's problem, and resending the same request is the right first move.
misconception.3: 200 means the request was fine. There is nothing to change.

steps.prompt: Your own handler throws, so no response is ever written. Which status do you return?
steps.feedback: 500, or a more specific 5xx, is the server saying the request was fine and handling it was not. Send it from the handler that caught the error.
